en: Thus have I heard: the Kīṭāgiri Sutta, the seventieth discourse in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kāsīs together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, I abstain from eating at night.”
“However, monks, by eating apart from the night-meal, I experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a state of well-being.
Come, monks, you too should eat apart from the night-meal.
By eating apart from the night-meal, you too will experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a state of well-being.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages on tour among the Kāsīs, arrived at a market town of the Kāsīs named Kīṭāgiri.
There the Blessed One stayed at Kīṭāgiri, the market town of the Kāsīs.
Now at that time, the monks named Assaji and Punabbasu were residents at Kīṭāgiri.
Then a number of monks approached the monks Assaji and Punabbasu; having approached, they said this to the monks Assaji and Punabbasu:
“Friends, the Blessed One and the community of monks refrain from eating at night.”
"But, friends, those who eat apart from eating at night experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling.
Come, friends, you too should eat apart from eating at night.
For, friends, by eating apart from eating at night, you too will experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling."
When this was said, the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka said to those bhikkhus:
"Friends, we eat both in the evening and in the morning, and during the day at the improper time.
Eating in the evening and in the morning, and during the day at the improper time, we experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling."
“Why should we abandon what is visible in this life and pursue what is temporal?
We shall eat both in the evening and in the morning, and during the day as well as at the improper time.
When those bhikkhus were unable to convince the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu, they then went to the Blessed One.
They approached him; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Sitting there to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, we went to where the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka were; having approached, we said this to the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka:"
“Friends, the Blessed One and the community of monks eat apart from eating at night.
By eating apart from eating at night, friends, they experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling.
Come, friends, you too should eat apart from eating at night.”
"But otherwise, friends, even you, by eating at night, will experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling.
When this was said, Bhante, the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka said this to us:
"Friends, we eat both in the evening, in the morning, and during the day at the improper time."

"Eating both in the evening and in the morning, as well as at improper times during the day, we experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a state of well-being.
Why should we abandon what is directly visible and pursue what belongs to the future?
We shall eat only in the evening and in the morning, and not at improper times."
“Since we, Bhante, were unable to convince the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka, we have now reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk:
“Come, monk, address the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka in my name, saying:”
“The Teacher summons you, venerable sirs.
“Very well, Bhante,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One, and he went to where the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu were. Having approached them, he said to the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu:
“The Teacher summons you, venerable sirs.”
“Yes, friend,” the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka replied to that bhikkhu, and they approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka were sitting there, the Blessed One said this to them:
“Is it true, monks, that many monks approached you and said this:
‘Friends, the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks eat apart from eating at night.
Now, friends, by eating apart from eating at night, they experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling.’”
"Come, friends, you too should eat apart from eating at night.
For by eating apart from eating at night, friends, you too will experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling.
When this was said, monks, you reportedly spoke thus to those bhikkhus:
“Moreover, friends, we eat both in the evening, in the morning, and at improper times during the day.
Eating thus in the evening, in the morning, and at improper times during the day, we experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a state of well-being.
Why should we abandon what is visible in this life and pursue what belongs to the future?”
“We shall eat in the evening, and in the morning, and at midday, and at the improper time.
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Bhikkhus, do you understand my Dhamma as taught by me in this way: ‘Whatever this person...’?”
“Does he experience pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, such that his unwholesome states diminish and his wholesome states increase?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Do you not understand, monks, this Dhamma taught by me thus:
that for some person here, when experiencing such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline;
whereas for another person here, when experiencing such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states [increase]?”
Unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline for someone here who experiences such a painful feeling;

however, for another person here who experiences such a painful feeling, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase. For yet another person here who experiences such a [painful feeling]...
"When one experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline;
yet here, for some who experience such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase."
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Good, monks.
Monks, had this been unknown by me, unseen, uncomprehended, unrealized, and untouched by wisdom:”
“Bhikkhus, if I did not know that for some person experiencing such a pleasant feeling unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,
would it be fitting for me to say, ‘Abandon such a pleasant feeling’? “No, indeed, Bhante.”
“But because, monks, this has been known by me, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom:
‘In this case, for someone experiencing such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline’—therefore I say: ‘Abandon such a pleasant feeling.
If, monks, this had not been known by me, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom:”

“Bhikkhus, if I were to say, ‘In this case, for someone experiencing such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,’ yet I did not know this, would it be proper for me to say, ‘Enter upon and abide in such a pleasant feeling’?”
“No, venerable sir.

“But because, monks, this has been known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by me with wisdom—namely, that for someone experiencing such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase—therefore I say: ‘Enter and abide in such a pleasant feeling.’”
"Monks, if this had not been known by me, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom—

that 'for someone experiencing such a painful feeling here, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline'— would it have been appropriate for me, monks, while not knowing this, to say: 'Abandon such a painful feeling'?"
“No, venerable sir.

“But because, monks, this has been known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by me with wisdom—namely, that for someone experiencing such a painful feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline—therefore I say: ‘Abandon such a painful feeling.’”
Bhikkhus, if this had not been known by me, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom— namely,
that “for someone experiencing such a painful feeling here, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase”—
then, not knowing this, I would have said: “Enter upon and abide in such a painful feeling.”
“Would it have been appropriate for me, monks, to do this?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“And because, monks, this has been known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by me through wisdom:”
"In this case, for someone experiencing such a painful feeling, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase. Therefore, I say: "Enter upon and abide in such a painful feeling.

And if, monks, this had not been known by me, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom—that "in this case, for someone experiencing such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase"—[I would not have said this].
“‘Wholesome states are declining’— if, not knowing this, I were to say, ‘Abandon such a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant,’ would that be appropriate for me, bhikkhus?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”

“However, monks, because this has been known by me, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom—namely, that ‘herein, for someone experiencing such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline’—therefore I say: ‘Abandon such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Monks, if this had not been known by me, unseen, unknown, unrealized, and untouched with wisdom:”
‘If, while someone here experiences such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase,’ were I not to know this,
I might say, ‘Enter and abide in such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’”
“Would it have been appropriate for me, monks, to do this?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“And because, monks, this has been known by me, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom:”
‘In this case, for someone experiencing such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
Therefore, I say: ‘Enter upon and abide in such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
“Monks, I do not say that ‘there is work to be done through diligence’ for all monks alike;
nor do I say, monks, that ‘there is no work to be done through diligence’ for all monks alike.
Those monks, monks, who are arahants with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, and laid down the burden...”

“Bhikkhus, for those bhikkhus who have realized the goal of the holy life, whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed, and who are liberated through right knowledge— for such bhikkhus, I say,
there is nothing further to be done by means of diligence. And why is that?”
For them, it has been accomplished through diligence;
they are incapable of negligence.

But as for those monks, bhikkhus, who are still in training (sekha), who have not yet attained their goal, and who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—it is for such monks, bhikkhus, that I say: "One must act with diligence."
And why is that? So that these venerable ones, by resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and harmonizing their faculties, might—

having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life— enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Monks, seeing this fruit of diligence for these monks, I say: ‘It is to be done with diligence.
Monks, there are these seven types of persons found existing in the world.
Which seven?”
The one liberated in both ways, the one liberated by wisdom, the body-witness, the one attained to view, the one liberated by faith, the Dhamma-follower, and the faith-follower.
And what, bhikkhus, is the person liberated in both ways?

Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells having personally realized with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend form, the formless attainments; and having seen them with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
“Monks, this person is called one liberated in both ways.
Monks, regarding this monk, I say: ‘There is nothing further to be done through heedfulness. And for what reason? Because he has already attained final knowledge (aññā) here and now.”
It has been said of him: "By means of diligence, he is incapable of negligence.
And who, monks, is the person liberated by wisdom?

"Here, monks, a certain person does not dwell having personally touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless and transcend form; yet, having seen them with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This person, monks, is called one liberated by wisdom.
And for this monk as well, monks, I say: 'There is nothing further to be done through diligence.'"
For what reason?
Because he has acted with diligence;
he is incapable of negligence.
"And what, bhikkhus, is the person who is a body-witness?

Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells having personally touched with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend form, which are formless; and having seen them with wisdom, some of his taints are utterly destroyed.
This, bhikkhus, is called the person who is a body-witness."
“Monks, I say that this monk has work to do with diligence.
And why? Perhaps this venerable one, while resorting to favorable lodgings, associating with good friends, and harmonizing his faculties, might [attain the goal].”

“May I, by realizing it for myself with direct knowledge, here and now enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
It is, monks, seeing this fruit of diligence for this monk that I say: “It is to be done through diligence.
And what kind of person, monks, is one who has attained view?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not dwell having personally touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless and transcend the realm of form;
yet, having seen them with wisdom, some of his taints are utterly destroyed,
and the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and mastered by him through wisdom.
This, monks, is called a person who has attained to view.
Yet, monks, I say of this monk as well: "He must still work with diligence. And why is that?

"Perhaps this venerable one, by resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and balancing his faculties, might—having realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life, having attained and entered upon it—the supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—dwell therein.
It is seeing this fruit of diligence for this bhikkhu, monks, that I say: "One must act with diligence."
And who, monks, is the person liberated by faith?
Here, monks, a certain person does not dwell having personally realized with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend the realm of form, the formless states;
yet, having seen them with wisdom, some of his taints are completely destroyed regarding the Tathāgata.
His faith is settled, rooted, and established.
This person, monks, is called one liberated by faith.
And for this monk as well, monks, I say: "It is to be done with diligence."
For what reason? It is because perhaps this venerable one, by resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and harmonizing his faculties, might—

having personally realized through direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal for which sons of noble family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness— dwell having attained it.
"Monks, seeing this fruit of diligence for this monk, I say: 'It is to be done through diligence.
And what kind of person, monks, is a follower by Dhamma?
Here, monks, a certain person does not [attain] those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms."
He dwells having touched [the truths] with the body; having seen them with wisdom, some of his taints are completely destroyed;
and the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are sufficiently accepted by him through wisdom after reflection; moreover, these qualities are present in him, namely:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
“Monks, this person is called a follower of the Dhamma.
And for this monk as well, monks, I say: ‘It is to be done with diligence.
For what reason? Because he has not yet attained the goal.”

"Perhaps this venerable one, by resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and harmonizing his faculties, might—having personally realized through direct knowledge in this very life the supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—abide having attained it.
It is, monks, seeing this fruit of diligence for this monk that I say: 'One must act with diligence.'"
And who, monks, is the person who follows by faith?
Here, monks, a certain person does not dwell having personally touched with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend the realm of form, the formless states;
yet, having seen them with wisdom, some of his taints are completely destroyed regarding the Tathāgata.
He possesses a measure of faith and a measure of affection, and he also possesses these qualities, namely:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
This, monks, is called a person who follows through faith.
“Monks, I say that this monk, too, must act with diligence.
And why? So that perhaps this venerable one, by resorting to favorable lodgings, associating with virtuous friends, and harmonizing his faculties, might—”

“May I, by realizing it for myself with direct knowledge, here and now enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
It is, monks, seeing this fruit of diligence for this monk that I say, “One should do what is to be done with diligence.
Monks, I do not say that the attainment of the goal comes about through the beginning alone;
Moreover, monks, there is gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress that leads to the attainment of the goal.
And how, monks, is there gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress that leads to the attainment of the goal?
Here, monks, one who has conceived faith approaches; approaching, he pays respectful attention; paying respectful attention...
He lends an ear; with an attentive ear he listens to the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he retains it; he examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained;
as he examines the meaning, the teachings become acceptable through reflection; when there is acceptance through reflection on the teachings, zeal arises;
being zealous, he exerts himself; having exerted himself, he investigates; having investigated, he strives; thus he becomes resolute.
Being thus concentrated, he realizes the supreme truth with his very body and, having penetrated it through wisdom, sees it.
Yet, monks, even that faith did not exist [before];
even that approach, monks, did not exist [before].
Even that, monks, was not an occasion for attendance;
even that, monks, was not an occasion for lending an ear;
even that, monks, was not an occasion for hearing the Dhamma.
Even that, monks, was not the retention of the Dhamma;
even that, monks, was not the investigation of the meaning;
even that, monks, was not the acceptance of the Dhamma after reflection.
Even that desire, monks, did not exist;
even that effort, monks, did not exist;
even that deliberation, monks, did not exist.
"Even that, monks, was not true striving.
You have gone astray, monks; you have practiced wrongly, monks.
How far indeed, monks, have these foolish men strayed from this Dhamma and Vinaya!"
“Bhikkhus, there is a four-line exposition which, when recited, a wise person would soon understand its meaning of wisdom.
I shall recite it to you, bhikkhus; will you understand it from me?
“Who are we, Bhante, and who are those who have understood the Dhamma?”
“Bhikkhus, even for a teacher who values material things, who is an heir to material things, and who dwells entangled with material things, such a reciprocal negotiation does not arise:
‘If it were thus for us, then we would do this; but if it were not thus for us, we would not do that. How much less, bhikkhus, for the Tathāgata, who dwells entirely unentangled with material things?
Bhikkhus, for a faithful disciple who has mastered the Teacher’s instruction and conducts himself accordingly, this is the natural consequence:”
‘The Blessed One is the Teacher, I am a disciple;
the Blessed One knows, I do not know.
For a faithful disciple who has mastered and conducts himself according to the Teacher’s instruction, monks, the Teacher’s instruction becomes established and full of essence.
“Bhikkhus, for a faithful disciple who has mastered the Teacher’s instruction and is practicing accordingly, this is the natural course of things:
‘Let only skin, sinew, and bone remain, and let the flesh and blood dry up in the body;
yet as long as I have not attained that which can be attained by human strength, human energy, and human perseverance, I shall not relax my effort.’”
‘...it will take shape.
Monks, for a faithful disciple who has mastered the Teacher’s instruction and conducts himself accordingly, one of two fruits may be expected:
final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The bhikkhus were uplifted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The *Kīṭāgirisutta*, the tenth, is finished.
The second chapter on the monks is finished.
Its summary verse is:
Kuñjara, Rāhula, Sassa, Taḷa, Loka.
Māluṅkyaputta and Bhaddāli by name;
Khuddaka, Diṭṭha, and Sahampati;
Nāḷaka and Rañña Kiṭāgiri by name.
